meta.description: Not Einstein. The line is John A. Shedd’s, printed in his 1928 aphorism collection Salt from My Attic. Grace Hopper later popularised a ‘port’ variant.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said ‘A Ship in Harbor Is Safe, But that Is Not What Ships Are Built For’?
meta.ogDescription: Not Einstein. The line is John A. Shedd’s, from his 1928 collection Salt from My Attic — Grace Hopper popularised it decades later.

answer.label: Not Albert Einstein — actually John A. Shedd
answer.authorDates: American aphorist · published ‘Salt from My Attic’ in 1928
answer.sourceLine: The aphorism was printed in Salt from My Attic, a slim collection of sayings compiled by John A. Shedd and published by The Mosher Press of Portland, Maine, in 1928 — on page 20, in almost exactly the wording that circulates today. Einstein is not connected to it by any contemporary source.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: A ship in harbor is safe, but that is not what ships are built for.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the saying to Shedd’s 1928 Salt from My Attic, citing page 20 of the Mosher Press edition and noting the citation was verified from photographic images of the book. Read the investigation ↗
Quote Investigator records that the same 1928 attribution to Shedd appears in Fred R. Shapiro’s Yale Book of Quotations. See the citation ↗

Wikiquote lists the ‘port’ variant in Grace Hopper’s Misattributed section and credits it to John Augustus Shedd, noting Hopper called it ‘a motto that has stuck with me’ and never claimed to have coined it. Wikiquote: Grace Hopper ↗

The earliest instance Quote Investigator finds crediting Einstein is a 1995 newspaper column — four decades after Einstein’s death in 1955, and some sixty-seven years after Shedd printed it. The 1995 citation ↗

author.name: John A. Shedd
author.heading: About John A. Shedd
author.metaLine: American aphorist · compiler of ‘Salt from My Attic’ (1928)
author.bio: John A. Shedd — given as John Augustus Shedd by Wikiquote — compiled Salt from My Attic, a collection of original sayings issued by Thomas Bird Mosher’s private press in Portland, Maine, in 1928. He left almost no biographical trace: the columnist Ed Howe, reprinting him in 1931, could describe him only as ‘an amateur’. One line from that slim book became one of the most quoted aphorisms in English, almost always under someone else’s name.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Three names get attached to this line. Only one of them wrote it.

items.why: No contemporary source connects Einstein to the saying. Quote Investigator calls the ascription ‘not substantive’ and finds it surfacing only in 1995, four decades after his death. Quote Investigator ↗
Hopper genuinely used a ‘ship in port’ variant — she gave one to the San Diego Union in 1981 — but she introduced it as a motto she had adopted, not one she wrote. Wikiquote: Grace Hopper ↗
Printed on page 20 of his 1928 collection Salt from My Attic, and reprinted with his name by the columnist Ed Howe in 1931. The 1928 citation ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Shedd wrote it in 1928; Hopper made it famous; Einstein never had anything to do with it. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Shedd’s book was a private-press curiosity — the columnist Ed Howe, reprinting several of its lines in 1931, introduced them as ‘sayings printed privately by an amateur named John A. Shedd’. The ship aphorism outlived the book completely.

What carried it was Grace Hopper. The computing pioneer quoted it for decades as a personal motto, and because she was the more famous name in the room, the saying gradually attached itself to her — and then, later still, to Einstein, the default author for any aphorism that sounds wise and has lost its owner.
context.pull: An amateur’s privately printed line outlived the book it came from.
